Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. For a witnessed-other-trauma presentation, the other threat items describe hypervigilance and startle around other people, and the triggers/memory/appraisal items do not suggest a home-intrusion or boundary-violation danger theme. Repeated door/window checking points to a specific safety behavior focused on securing the environment, which is not supported elsewhere in the selected items and does not fit the formulation well, especially given that maladaptive-strategy links are inactive.

vignette:
Kimo is a 71-year-old cashier at a busy supermarket in Honolulu, married for forty-seven years to his wife, Leilani. Three years ago, on a humid evening during his shift, a man walked through the automatic doors and within seconds shot a customer in the checkout line over a trivial argument. Kimo stood frozen at his register, ten feet away. The customer collapsed; the shooter fled. A young woman with a baby was standing nearby, and the baby began to wail—a high, piercing cry that seemed to go on for hours. In reality it was only a few minutes until paramedics arrived, but that sound has never left him. The perpetrator was never caught. Store management told employees not to discuss the incident and offered no counseling; the police investigation went nowhere. To Kimo, the people who should have protected him—the store, the security guards who arrived too late, the police who never made an arrest—simply failed. The shooter faced no consequences, and that felt like a second wound.

Since that night, Kimo’s memory of the event has remained fractured. He can recall the door sliding open and the argument, but the order of what happened next is a blur. When Leilani asks him about it, he starts to explain, then loses the thread—the words scatter. He cannot tell a clear story even to himself; there are gaps where the terror should be, only a blank. He has stopped trying.

At work, the automatic doors are a constant source of dread. Each time they slide open or slam shut, his body jerks as if the shooter has returned. Unexpected movement—a customer reaching quickly for a wallet, a child darting past him—triggers the same jolt, flooding him with adrenaline and the conviction that danger is imminent. He has become hypervigilant, scanning every face and hand in the checkout line, watching for any sign of threat. He reads hostility in ordinary gestures: a man adjusting his jacket, a woman shifting a bag. Kimo knows this is irrational, but he cannot stop. The sound of a baby crying—any baby, anywhere in the store—sends a spike of fear through him, instantly transporting him back to that high-pitched wail mixed with the gunshots.

He has grown emotionally numb. He feels dead inside, going through the motions of work and family life without any real connection. Leilani has noticed he no longer laughs at her jokes, no longer reaches for her hand. He avoids the back aisle of the store where the incident occurred, but as a cashier he must stay at the front, near the doors. He has asked his manager to let him work in the back office, but his seniority doesn’t allow it, and he cannot explain why without tearing up. Instead, he endures each shift in a state of coiled tension, taking frequent breaks in the stockroom to calm his racing heart.

What finally brought Kimo to seek help was an incident two weeks ago: a customer moved unexpectedly toward him to grab a dropped receipt, and Kimo shouted at him to get back. The customer complained to management, and Kimo was written up. Leilani insisted he see a therapist. He agreed, but inside he fears that talking will bring back the parts of the memory he cannot piece together, and that he will never feel alive again. He hopes, barely, that someone can help him make sense of it—that maybe, after all this time, he can find a way to live without watching every movement, waiting for the next door to slam.
